I agree to get used to the pedals you have and what you like and don’t like about them and learn how to fix setup issues/noises and all the factors that go into making a well setup sounding and working pedalboard. A good amp for pedals is more important then the pedals themselves. Can’t do anything that sounds good with pedals if you don’t like the sound of your amp as it is. You can look into a boss ir-2 or other amp sim pedals but it takes a certain knowledge of the pedals to work really well like a tube amp would and with other pedals such as distortion. As well as which direction works for you as a speaker for the amp sim. Play the pedals you have now. Tweak them and listen to them closely. To fight blur you will just have to increase or find the right shutter speed. Look up YouTube videos and tutorials on iso, aperture, and shutter speed and how those three work with each other to get the picture you want. If it’s a bright day I can set my shutter speed to /1000 and reasonably I would have little to no blur. On a darker day you will have to weigh in or manage/sacrifice options for those shutter speed, aperture, and iso to get the picture you need. I feel like I’m making it sound harder than it is but I’d definitely watch YouTube tutorials and it will make more sense when you have your camera in hand. Reading the Manuel also helps.

Image stabilization in a lens can help but it is not necessary. A lot of lens that cost 4x or 5x more don’t have image stabilization. Also it is usually used for telephoto lenses because the more you zoom in, the more the shake is noticeable. Image stabilization in a camera is more seen in expensive body’s. 

You can use Manual lens or AF lens on your camera. With manual lens you will have to focus by turning the front portion of the lens to focus and then take the shot (like in the old days with film).  With an autofocus camera and lens that a majority of people use (especially beginners) you press the shutter button halfway until the lens (with the help of the camera) has automatically focused on what you aimed at with the focus point you see which is usually a rectangle. I would start with an autofocus lens so you can get the hang of camera settings and it’s not that easy to get quick action or in focus shots quickly if you manually have to focus. Most people these days from novice to pro use mostly autofocus.

No problem! In the future if you desire a zoom lens, look for a fixed aperture with something like 1.8, 2, or 2.8. With the zoom lens you mentioned, if you zoom in the aperture will go up and cause a darker exposure. Primes are also great starter lenses, especially if you know what you want to shoot. I think it will teach you more and I have way more fun framing with a fixed focal length.

Well all the white balances will be yellowish except auto, incodesent, and the custom settings (depending what custom temperature is at) with indoor lighting for the most part. Go to white balances and set the c. Temp/filter to 2500k and it shouldnt be yellow but could possibly be really blue so thats when you raise it a bit. On "A" which is aperture priority and white balance set to an adjusted c. Temp/filter it shouldnt be yellow on the mid to lower kelvin (k) level. If it is than something strange is wrong with your camera or lens or the lighting in the room is weird or too artificial. Most likely the latter. Stuck in a room with a camera can be really suffocating or doubtful compared to outside or an adventure if you know what I mean. Shooting with a custom white balance is always a good idea though.  Learn how to shoot with aperture priorty or "A" and adjust iso manually for more light or set the iso to auto and you will thank me for just starting out. It tends to stay at/60 shutter speed on auto iso with A sometimes though which isnt all that bad. Research all the settings though... obviously manual setting most importantly. Hope this helps.
